explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model hits a content‐bearing “anchor” word—i.e. a key noun or technical term (named entity, loanword or jargon) that introduces or labels the main topic of a span, across languages and formats.

This neuron fires on content-heavy technical terms—i.e. the specialized jargon or keywords that name core concepts (in physics, math, programming, config files, web dev, etc.) across a variety of technical documents.

This neuron fires on the “header” or top‐matter of a document—things like copyright/license blocks, generated-by comments, class/interface declarations or court-case title lines—i.e. the metadata and section-heading text that appears at the very beginning of files or legal filings.

This feature lights up on the first token immediately following an opening quotation delimiter (e.g. “, 「, or the quote marks around a string literal), marking the start of a quoted span across languages and contexts.

This neuron fires on the very first “content‐word” that begins a new structural block—be it the opening verb of a news paragraph, the lead term in an abstract (e.g. “We,” “This work”), the key method name (“Monte” in “Monte Carlo”), a citation identifier or .bib filename, the first volume/page number in a reference, the first entry after a msgstr, etc. In short, it marks the head token that kicks off a fresh section or entry.

Here’s a concise concept summary for each starred feature:

• Perm  
  Picks up the root “perm-” in words about official permissions (permit, permitting) in bureaucratic/legal contexts.  

• Religion  
  Marks mentions of “religion” or “religious,” especially in church–state/legal event discussions.  

• CAS  
  Detects the Spanish plural noun “casos” (cases), typically in legal/human-rights reporting.  

• Revers  
  Flags the prefix “revers-” in scientific terms (reversibility of processes).  

• Appro  
  Triggers on “approv-” stems (approve, approves) denoting formal approval actions.  

• RE  
  Targets the prefix “RE,” as used in titles or remakes (RE2, re-presenting).  

• action  
  Catches the suffix “-action” (primarily in “reaction”), covering chemical reactions or brand names using “Reaction.”  

• Donald  
  Spotlights the substring “-Donald” in surnames (MacDonald, etc.).  

• François  
  Identifies the French given name “François,” including its diacritic.  

• Hen  
  Fires on the “Hen-” beginning of names (Henri, Henrietta).  

• Corporate  
  Picks up the word “corporate,” here in the context of business/travel.  

• ance  
  Flags the noun suffix “-ance” as in “romance.”  

• ton  
  Marks the substring “-ton” in place-names (Downton).

This feature detects boundary punctuation—specifically the “.” and “?” tokens—that mark the ends of sentences (questions or statements) or serve as separators (e.g. in dot‐qualified names and imports).
This neuron is a pure orthographic detector for short, uncommon subword chunks—often acronyms or rare letter‐only sequences (e.g. “ph,” “ID,” “PLE,” “ø,” “uff,” etc.) regardless of semantic domain.

This feature fires on the little substrings that make up publication and section names, datelines, and other news‐article metadata—e.g. “Cr” in TechCrunch, “Ins” in Business Insider, “Rele” in Press Releases, “sw” in Newswise, “fr” in San Francisco, “AG” in CHICAGO, “fol” in portfolios—so it is detecting the structural markers of a news or press‐release style document.

This neuron lights up on the little bits of “glue” that separate and format pieces in technical/markdown prose—periods after list numbers, commas in numeric lists, hyphens in ranges or model names, the `---` of YAML front-matter or section breaks, and the `**…**` markers for bold. It’s essentially a delimiter/formatting-token detector.

This neuron fires on little navigational markers in formal texts—things like “next-page” numbers in law-report headers or bracketed footnote tags in academic papers. In other words, it picks up on the tiny numeric/annotational tokens (page-continuation figures, footnote reference labels, etc.) that structure and link sections of a document.

The feature fires on sentence- or line-initial, capitalized “heading” words—often methodological or action-oriented terms—that introduce sections or titles (e.g. Quantitative, Evaluation, Analysis, Changes, Comparison, Risk, Increased) or UI prompts (Watch, More like this).

This neuron flags tokens containing non-Latin script characters—e.g. CJK ideographs, Hebrew/Arabic-script letters, Cyrillic, etc.—typically found in comments or string literals when foreign‐language text appears in code or docs.

This neuron fires on the little “joiners” you see in tightly‐formatted, domain-specific names and codes—chiefly the hyphens (and occasionally other punctuation like colons) that glue together acronyms, numbers, gene- or protein-subunits, chemical groups, case IDs, method names, etc., in scientific, legal or technical nomenclature.

This neuron detects the core semantic sub‐word (the root or stem) of content-bearing tokens—be they Greek/Latin technical roots (gly-, chrom-, zyg-, ochrom-, ster-, etc.), numerals in scientific notation (10, 4, 5…), key substrings in proper names (arczyk, –ekstan, год-), or classifying nouns (village). In effect it fires on the central morpheme that carries a word’s main meaning across languages and domains.

This feature fires on named‐label tokens—i.e. the user-defined identifiers that introduce or anchor things, whether they’re Markdown/LaTeX section IDs (`{#Sec1}`, `{#s0001}`), HTML-style anchors, or code symbols (class, trait, method or variable names like `AnyRef`, `resize`, `writeFileSync`, `On_BeginRequest`, `TranslationKeyRepository`, etc.). In short, it flags tokens that serve as unique labels or definitions in docs and source.

The feature is a “capital‐letter/Unicode‐surrogate” detector: it fires on tokens beginning with an uppercase character (in any script) or the replacement-character �, thereby marking sentence starts, proper names, acronyms, and instances of mojibake or decoding artifacts.

This neuron seems to fire on tokens that kick off a new structured unit—be it the head of a mathematical sub‐expression (e.g. the “sqrt” call or the “***” exponent operator), the first word of a legal heading (“In” at the start of a case caption), the opening name in a counsel listing, or even the initial pronoun in a new narrative (“His”).  In other words, it marks the entry point of sub‐expressions, headings or parenthetical/listing clauses across very different domains.

This neuron fires on morphemes expressing totality or boundary/extremal quantification (all-/every-/nothing-/always-/beyond-/before-/after- etc.) across languages, flagging words that denote complete inclusion, exclusion, or temporal/spatial extremes.

This feature is a cue for formal research‐style discourse—section headings and methodological terms you’d see in academic or clinical papers (e.g. “Discussion,” “Introduction,” “meta‐analysis,” “case studies,” “assessment,” “contraindications,” etc.), marking the structure and jargon of scholarly reporting.
This feature detects calendar‐style date expressions (day–month–year mentions) in text.
This feature is a detector for the opening single‐quote that marks the very start of an abstract’s quoted text (i.e. the leading ‘ after “abstract:”) in LaTeX‐style academic papers.

This neuron is basically a “word‐ending” detector: it fires on tokens that form the final subword piece (or a standalone monosyllabic root) of a word—whether that’s a true suffix in a longer word (or, ul, ip, per, iz, etc.) or a complete one-syllable word (point, fear, one, worries).

This neuron lights up on continuation subword pieces of specialized jargon—i.e. the non-initial stems or affixes in technical terms and abbreviations (e.g. “ureus” in Cureus, “encephal” in magnetoencephalography, “athione” in glutathione, “nerg” in synergistic, “F” in legal citations, “G” in Gamer)—flagging domain-specific vocabulary.

This neuron is a “title/heading” detector – it lights up on the first tokens of article or section titles (news headlines, blog‐post or doc headings, markdown bold/underscore titles, etc.) across languages.

This neuron is a sub-word “morpheme detector” for Greek/Latin roots that recur in technical jargon—e.g. “pat” in patent/Patreon, “rost” in prosthetic, “cyt” in cytotoxic, “orth” in orthogonal, “anth” in anthropogenic, “dyst” in dystrophin, “pyreth” in pyrethroid, etc. It lights up on the characteristic root‐letter sequences that signal specialized scientific, medical or legal terms.
This feature is simply detecting the BPE subword “ok” (and its close variant “ö” in some languages) – e.g. the “ok” piece in Novak, Djokovic, Yokohama, Nokton, Oktoberfest, Bokmässan, Nokogiri, etc.

This feature responds to high-level discourse markers and section anchors—words that introduce or frame chunks of content (e.g. headings, intros, disclaimers, calls-to-action or transition cues). It highlights tokens like “Being,” “Our,” “contains,” “Description,” “will,” etc., which signal new sections, summarize or qualify material, and guide the reader through the text.
This neuron is firing on the head‐of‐predicate in a clause—the central action or state word (whether a verb, adjective or deverbal noun) that carries the sentence’s core proposition.

This feature lights up on title-case tokens—especially the connective “Of” in list-style headlines and the first words of proper names or branded titles—marking the boundaries of capitalized phrases in headings.

This feature fires on BPE tokens that begin with an uppercase letter (often followed by lowercase letters), i.e. the word-initial capitalized prefixes you see in titles, proper names, legal headings and brand or magazine names.

Here’s a concise abstract for each highlighted token, capturing the general concept the feature appears to mark:

1. delicate  
   – A refined sensory adjective in luxury product descriptions (subtle, soft fragrance).

2. rationale  
   – The notion of non-integer (rational) indexing in numerical array operations.

3. interpolation  
   – Mathematical interpolation methods (e.g. spline, linear) in scientific computing.

4. consultants  
   – External personnel category governed by corporate policy rules.

5. jquery  
   – The inclusion and usage pattern of the jQuery JavaScript library in web pages.

6. Enable  
   – A user-interface toggle command that activates a particular software feature.

7. athletic  
   – An official role or title within sports administration and team contexts.

8. auditory  
   – The anatomical subsystem related to hearing pathways in neurobiology.

9. colorful  
   – Vivid descriptive language used to enliven narrative or historical writing.

10. templates  
    – Prebuilt design assets (HTML/CSS) provided for rapid web development.

11. suburban  
    – A geographic/demographic qualifier in educational or statistical reporting.

12. 1938  
    – A numeric year label denoting the date of a historical artifact.

13. celebrate  
    – Promotional framing language for anniversary or milestone events.

14. incentives  
    – Policy-driven financial motivators designed to influence behavior.

15. tools  
    – Versioned developer utility components in a software ecosystem.

16. command  
    – Named operations or aliases in an interactive debugger environment.

17. functionality  
    – A discrete software capability module (e.g. video-chat API feature).

18. orthogonal  
    – A geometric/orientation specification in simulation or modeling setups.

This neuron is a “subtoken” detector – it lights up whenever the model sees a common BPE fragment (roots or affixes) or code‐keyword piece rather than a full word. Examples include the English “enc” (in agency, sentences, Valencia), the code keyword “import,” Russian endings like “ическ,” Polish/Thai subword chunks, the root “arcin” in carcinogens, and so on. Essentially it flags mid‐word or domain‐specific subword units.

This neuron fires on the main technical noun of a sentence or title in scientific/engineering text—i.e. the key domain‐specific object, procedure or concept (equipment names, anatomical structures, operations, syndromes, etc.) that marks the topic of the statement.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on the very first “content” word following an opening indefinite article (“A”/“An”)—whether that word is an adjective (hybrid, defining, quantitative), a numeral in an age–year construction (56-, 78-, 20-, 15-, 60-year-old), a study or object noun (Bill), or other head-noun/subword in “A …” noun phrases. In effect it marks the core descriptor that kicks off titles, abstracts or case-report intros.

This neuron seems to light up on the very tokens that introduce or highlight the main topic or “head” of a noun‐phrase or headline across languages—whether that’s a quantifier (“MORE”), an indefinite article in German (“ein”), a key noun (“Hunger”), a modal (“might”), a brand or team name (“SHIELD,” “Rams”), or the crucial subword in a compound (“autol-,” “yl,” “OWN”). In short, it marks the token that launches a new, salient entity or focus in news-style and informational text.

This neuron is a detector for document‐level metadata/headers—things like page or section markers, legal‐case citations (volumes, reporters, years), copyright lines, date/time stamps and other formal identifiers that typically sit at the top or bottom of pages or sections.

This neuron fires on attributive‐modifier tokens that kick off noun phrases or clauses—e.g. possessive pronouns (my), quantifiers (several), adjectives (small, old), discourse adverbs (apparently) and even adjective suffix subwords (##mental, ##whelming). It flags words that introduce or qualify the following phrase.

This neuron fires on structural‐metadata tokens in formal or semi‐structured text—primarily standalone numbers (case or section identifiers, list or edition labels, phone codes) and the headings that accompany them (e.g. “Introduction,” “Additional Information”). It flags the markers authors use to organize documents.

This neuron fires on generic technical labels for discrete components or parameters in structured, often patent- or code-style writing—words like “module,” “path,” “value,” “level,” “terminal,” “region,” “entity,” “settings,” etc., used to name the building blocks or configurable elements of a system.
